item.title: Spotting Right and Wrong Conduct Under Standard III
item.summary: Standard III sets out what you owe your clients: loyalty, fair treatment, suitable advice, honest performance numbers and privacy. This lesson trains you to look at a short scenario and decide quickly whether the conduct fits the Standards or breaks them.

sections.heading: A sorting habit for scenario questions
sections.body_markdown:
Exam questions in this area give you a short story and ask whether someone **conformed** or **violated**. Run each story through four quick checks:

1. **Whose interest came first?** The client's, or the adviser's or firm's?
2. **Were all clients treated fairly?** Fair does not mean identical, but nobody should be quietly favoured.
3. **Did the action fit the client's written objectives and constraints?**
4. **Was information, whether performance data or client details, shown honestly and kept private?**

The five parts of Standard III map onto these checks: III(A) Loyalty, Prudence and Care; III(B) Fair Dealing; III(C) Suitability; III(D) Performance Presentation; III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality. Many wrong answers are not wildly unethical. They are conduct that is nearly right but leaves out one required piece, such as a disclosure.

sections.heading: III(A) and III(B): loyalty and fair treatment
sections.body_markdown:
**Loyalty, prudence and care** is a minimum standard that applies to every member and candidate, whether or not a legal fiduciary duty also applies. If you hold **custody** (any direct or indirect access to client money) or manage a pool of assets, the governing documents, such as a trust deed or investment management agreement, are the main source of your powers and duties. Acting against them puts you at risk of violating III(A).

**Fair dealing** means being even-handed when you give analysis, make recommendations or trade. Think of a restaurant that serves every table from the same kitchen: it can offer a pricier tasting menu, but it can't hand the best dishes to the owner's friends first.

- **Conforms:** a clearly disclosed service tier that any client can buy; releasing a rating change to all clients at the same time; allocating a limited offering fairly across accounts.
- **Violates:** sending a new recommendation to a few favoured contacts before the full client list; steering the best trades to accounts that pay performance fees; putting the firm's own convenience ahead of a client's outcome.

sections.heading: III(C): suitability
sections.body_markdown:
Before recommending or acting in an advisory relationship, you must make a **reasonable inquiry** into the client's investment experience, risk and return objectives and financial constraints. You must update that information regularly and confirm that the investment is suitable and consistent with the client's **written** objectives, mandates and constraints. These are usually collected in an **investment policy statement (IPS)**.

A good test is to judge the fit of an investment inside the whole portfolio and the IPS, not on its own appeal.

- **Violates:** buying an exciting, high-risk holding for a client whose IPS stresses capital preservation; never revisiting the client's profile after major life changes.
- **Conforms:** choosing an investment that fits the IPS, even if it ranks second on pure financial-statement metrics. Looking at other factors, such as ESG criteria, is allowed when they support the client's risk and return objectives.

sections.heading: III(D): performance presentation
sections.body_markdown:
When you communicate performance, you must make reasonable efforts to make it **fair, accurate and complete**. This covers individual accounts, composites (a combined record of similar portfolios) and pooled funds you claim responsibility for. Research analysts must meet the same bar when they promote how accurate their recommendations have been.

**Conforms:**
- Showing a track record from a prior employer, with clear disclosure of where it was earned and your actual role.
- Labelling simulated or model results as simulated.
- Using a composite of similar portfolios that includes terminated accounts.
- Stating whether returns are gross or net of fees, or after tax.
- Making supporting detail available on request when the presentation is brief.

**Violates:**
- Passing off a former firm's results as the current firm's.
- Presenting back-tested results as though they were real.
- Building a composite from hand-picked accounts, or changing its membership to flatter results.
- Using one star account to represent the strategy.

Following the GIPS standards is the best route to compliance, but it is not the only one.

sections.heading: III(E): confidentiality

worked_example.problem: Sort each situation as conforming or violating. (1) An adviser joins a new firm and shows a five-year record from her old employer, labelled as earned there, with a description of her role. (2) A portfolio manager e-mails a revised Buy recommendation to three golf partners who are clients, and publishes it to everyone else the next day. (3) A retiree's IPS stresses capital preservation and low volatility, and the adviser places a large part of the portfolio in one speculative stock without discussing it with the client. (4) After a client leaves the firm, the adviser tells a friend at a rival firm about the former client's holdings.
steps: Apply the four checks. For (1), ask whether the performance was shown honestly. Source and role are disclosed, so III(D) is satisfied. Conforms.
For (2), ask whether clients were treated fairly. A select group got the recommendation first, so this breaks III(B). Violates.
For (3), ask whether the action fit the written objectives. A concentrated speculative holding contradicts the IPS, so this breaks III(C), and it also raises III(A) concerns. Violates.
For (4), ask whether the information stayed private. A former client is still protected and no exception applies, so this breaks III(E). Violates.
worked_example.answer: Only situation (1) conforms; situations (2), (3) and (4) violate Standard III.

exam_traps: Believing that fair dealing means treating every client identically. Different service levels are acceptable if they are disclosed and available to all; secretly giving some clients a head start is not.
Thinking performance from a previous employer can never be shown. It can, provided the source and your specific role are disclosed.
Treating simulated or back-tested results as acceptable because the underlying method is sound. They must be clearly labelled as simulated.
Judging suitability by how attractive an investment is on its own. The test is fit with the client's written objectives, constraints and total portfolio.

Assuming a client's confidentiality ends when the relationship ends, or that it can never be broken. Former clients are protected, but disclosure is allowed for illegal activity, legal requirement or client permission.

Standard I(A) Knowledge of the Law

item.stem: A portfolio manager moves to a new firm and wants to include her six-year equity record from her previous employer in the new firm's marketing. Which approach conforms to Standard III(D)?

options.text: Show the record without naming the prior employer so the new firm looks established.
options.explanation: Omitting the source misleads prospects about where and by whom the results were achieved. This is a misrepresentation, so it violates III(D).

options.text: Do not show it at all, because past results from another firm can never be used.
options.explanation: This is too strict. Showing a prior-firm record is allowed when properly disclosed.

options.text: Show it, stating clearly that it was earned at the prior firm and what her role was.
options.explanation: Correct. Past performance from a previous firm can be presented if the source and the individual's specific role are fully disclosed.

item.stem: Which of the following is most likely a violation of Standard III(D) when a firm presents performance for a balanced strategy?

options.text: Including terminated accounts in the composite and stating that returns are net of fees.
options.explanation: Including terminated accounts and disclosing the fee basis are recommended practices for fair, complete presentation, so this conforms.

options.text: Showing the results of the single best-performing account as representative of the strategy.
options.explanation: Correct. Using one hand-picked account rather than a composite of similar portfolios gives a distorted, incomplete picture.

options.text: Giving a brief summary that notes its limited nature and offers full supporting data on request.
options.explanation: Brief presentations are acceptable when supporting details are available on request, and noting their limits is best practice. This conforms.

item.stem: Which of the following conduct conforms to Standard III(B) Fair Dealing?

options.text: Phoning a few large clients about a rating change before posting it for all other clients.
options.explanation: Giving some clients earlier access to a recommendation disadvantages the rest. This is the classic fair-dealing violation.

options.text: Placing oversubscribed offering shares first in accounts that pay performance fees.
options.explanation: Favouring higher-fee accounts in allocations is unfair to other clients and violates III(B).

options.text: Offering a disclosed premium research tier that every client may choose to buy.
options.explanation: Correct. Fair dealing does not mean identical service. Different service levels are acceptable when disclosed and open to all clients.

item.stem: An adviser's retired client has a written IPS focused on capital preservation and low risk. Which action is most likely a violation of Standard III(C)?

options.text: Recommending a speculative stock because of its high stand-alone expected return, ignoring the IPS risk limits.
options.explanation: Correct. Suitability requires consistency with the client's written objectives and constraints, not attractiveness in isolation.

options.text: Assessing whether a proposed holding fits within the client's total portfolio and IPS.
options.explanation: Judging fit within the whole portfolio and the IPS is exactly what suitability requires, so this conforms.

options.text: Asking the client to update personal circumstances and risk tolerance after a change in health.
options.explanation: Regularly reassessing and updating client information is required by III(C), so this conforms.

item.stem: A family-office manager has an IPS aiming at long-term capital preservation and downside-risk control. Company X looks slightly better on financial statements, but Company Y scores far higher on ESG criteria, which the manager believes lowers its risk. He buys Company Y. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: He violated the Standards because choices must rest on financial statement analysis alone.
options.explanation: Nothing in the Standards limits selection to financial-statement metrics, so this misreads III(C).

options.text: He violated the Standards because ESG factors can only be used if the client explicitly requests them.
options.explanation: No separate client request is required. The test is consistency with the IPS objectives.

options.text: He conformed, because non-financial factors such as ESG may be used if the choice suits the IPS.
options.explanation: Correct. The manager must pick investments suitable for the IPS and may consider criteria beyond financial metrics, including ESG.

item.stem: An investment adviser stops managing money for a client. Which later action conforms to Standard III(E) Preservation of Confidentiality?

options.text: Telling authorities about the former client's plan to commit a financial crime, after learning of it during the relationship.
options.explanation: Correct. Information concerning illegal activity by the client is an exception to the duty of confidentiality, so limited disclosure is permitted.

options.text: Telling a contact at another firm about the former client's holdings, as the relationship has ended.
options.explanation: Confidentiality covers former clients too. Ending the relationship does not free the adviser to talk.

options.text: Mentioning the former client's net worth to a business prospect to show the quality of past clients.
options.explanation: Using client details as a marketing tool is not covered by any exception, so this violates III(E).

item.stem: A candidate manages a client trust whose governing document restricts the portfolio to investment-grade bonds. Believing it will earn more, she invests 10% in a speculative equity fund. She reasons that her prudent judgment justifies it and that she will tell the trustees afterwards. Which assessment is most accurate?

options.text: No violation, because prudent judgment can override the document when it is likely to raise returns.
options.explanation: Prudence does not allow ignoring the governing document. Treating her own judgment as superior to the document is the error.

options.text: A violation of III(A), because governing documents are the primary determinant of her powers and duties.
options.explanation: Correct. Acting contrary to the trust instrument puts her in breach of loyalty, prudence and care, regardless of her return expectations.

options.text: No violation, because disclosure to the trustees after the trade cures the breach.
options.explanation: After-the-fact disclosure does not make an unauthorized investment acceptable. The action itself breaches the mandate.

item.front: What three qualities must performance information have under Standard III(D)?
item.back: It must be fair, accurate and complete, and members must make reasonable efforts to ensure this.

item.front: Can you show performance earned at a previous employer in new marketing material?
item.back: Yes, if you clearly disclose where the results were earned and your specific role in achieving them. Hiding the source violates III(D).

item.front: Does fair dealing under III(B) mean every client gets exactly the same treatment?
item.back: No. Different service levels are fine if disclosed and open to all, but giving some clients early or better access in secret is a violation.

item.front: What are the three exceptions to the III(E) duty of confidentiality?
item.back: The information concerns illegal activity, disclosure is required by law, or the client permits disclosure. The duty covers current, former and prospective clients.

warnings: 1/7 items have the longest option as the key
